problem: The parameter is named iterable, but the sentence then says set(iterable) builds a set from 'any sequence'. A sequence is narrower than an iterable; a range, a generator, a dict or a file can all be passed to set(). The mismatch can confuse students about what is allowed.
fix: The constructor set(iterable) builds a set from any iterable — a list, a string, a range, a generator or a dict — and drops duplicates silently.

where: Section 3, paragraph 2, and Exam traps bullet 4
problem: The chapter says the four arithmetic operators need a set on both sides and illustrates only A | [7, 8]. The comparison operators behave the same way; A <= [1, 2] also raises TypeError. A student may believe list arguments are fine on the right of <=.
fix: Add one sentence: the comparison operators <=, >=, < and > also need a set on the other side; A <= [1, 2] raises TypeError, while A.issubset([1, 2]) accepts any iterable.

problem: 'x in A costs about the same for ten items and for ten lakh items' is true only on average. If many keys collide, for example objects with equal hashes, the lookup degrades towards comparing items one by one. Calling the cost constant without the average-case qualifier overstates the guarantee.
fix: On average, x in A costs about the same for ten items and for ten lakh items, because Python hashes x, computes a slot and looks there; if many keys collide, the cost can grow towards O(n).
